section.title: The Dreams in Prison
section.sectionRationale: In prison Joseph meets Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker, who each dream a troubling dream. Insisting that interpretations belong to God, Joseph reads the dreams truly: restoration for one, execution for the other. His plea to be remembered goes unanswered, and the chapter closes on a forgotten man in a dungeon.
section.thesis: God, not human wisdom, reveals and rules the future; He gives Joseph true interpretations even in prison, yet ordains that his release must wait on God's timing rather than on a grateful man's memory.
section.frameNote: Four movements: two royal prisoners and their dreams; the cupbearer's dream interpreted; the baker's dream interpreted; and the dreams fulfilled on Pharaoh's birthday, with Joseph forgotten.

verses.text: Some time later, the king’s cupbearer and baker offended their master, the king of Egypt.
Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker,
and imprisoned them in the house of the captain of the guard, the same prison where Joseph was confined.
The captain of the guard assigned them to Joseph, and he became their personal attendant. After they had been in custody for some time,
both of these men, the Egyptian king’s cupbearer and baker, who were being held in the prison, had a {{chalom|dream}} on the same night, and each dream had its own meaning.
When Joseph came to them in the morning, he saw that they were distraught.
So he asked the officials of Pharaoh who were in custody with him in his master’s house, “Why are your faces so downcast today?”
“We both had dreams,” they replied, “but there is no one to interpret them.” Then Joseph said to them, “Don’t {{pithron|interpretations}} belong to God? Tell me your dreams.”
So the chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream: “In my dream there was a vine before me,
and on the vine were three branches. As it budded, its blossoms opened and its clusters ripened into grapes.
Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes, squeezed them into his cup, and placed the cup in his hand.”
Joseph replied, “This is the interpretation: The three branches are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore your position. You will put Pharaoh’s cup in his hand, just as you did when you were his cupbearer.
But when it goes well for you, please {{zakar|remember}} me and show me kindness by mentioning me to Pharaoh, that he might bring me out of this prison.
For I was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews, and even here I have done nothing for which they should have put me in this dungeon.”

units.label: The baker's dream
units.note: a favorable start, a fatal end

verses.text: When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, “I too had a dream: There were three baskets of white bread on my head.
In the top basket were all sorts of baked goods for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head.”
Joseph replied, “This is the interpretation: The three baskets are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will lift off your head and hang you on a tree. Then the birds will eat the flesh of your body.”
On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he held a feast for all his officials, and in their presence he {{nasarosh|lifted up the heads}} of the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.
Pharaoh restored the chief cupbearer to his position, so that he once again placed the cup in Pharaoh’s hand.
But Pharaoh hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had described to them in his interpretation.
The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him.

chalom.gloss: A dream. Dreams structure the whole Joseph story, and here two God-given dreams in a single night set the stage for Joseph's eventual rise. In Genesis, dreams are a means by which God discloses what He is about to do, so their true interpretation belongs to Him alone.

pithron.gloss: Interpretation, the meaning of a dream. Joseph deflects glory from himself with the question, do not interpretations belong to God, setting Israel's God above the celebrated dream-diviners of Egypt. The word ties this chapter to the next, where the same God-given gift lifts Joseph before Pharaoh.

zakar.gloss: To remember, to call to mind and act upon. Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember him, but the man forgets, verse 23. The contrast is pointed: human memory fails, yet God will remember Joseph in His own time, as He remembered Noah and the covenant, driving the story toward deliverance.

nasarosh.gloss: To lift up the head. Joseph uses this idiom two ways: for the cupbearer it means restoration and honor, for the baker a grim reversal, to lift off the head in execution. On Pharaoh's birthday both are lifted up, one to life and one to death, a sober wordplay on the two destinies decided by the king.

basic.context: Still in prison, Joseph is put in charge of two of Pharaoh's officials who have fallen out of favor, the cupbearer and the baker. Each has a dream on the same night. Joseph interprets them: the cupbearer will be restored, the baker executed, both within three days. It happens just as he said, but the cupbearer forgets him.
basic.hermeneutics: The key question is who holds the future and its meaning. Joseph answers plainly: interpretations belong to God. The chapter is not about Joseph's cleverness but about the God who reveals what He is about to do and governs the timing of everything, including Joseph's release.
basic.originalLanguages: Dreams are God's chosen way of disclosing His plans here, and their interpretation belongs to Him. Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember him, but the man forgets, while God will remember Joseph in His time. The phrase lift up the head is used two ways, for the cupbearer's honor and the baker's execution.
basic.typology: The two prisoners, one saved and one condemned on the same day, foreshadow the two criminals crucified beside Jesus, and the plea remember me anticipates the thief's cry to Christ. The three days and the lifting up quietly echo the pattern of death and resurrection.
basic.christ: Joseph, the innocent prisoner who announces salvation and judgment, points to Christ, between whom two condemned men met opposite ends. One asked Jesus to remember him and was received into paradise. The three days and the lifting up whisper of the greater deliverance won at the cross and empty tomb.
basic.god: God is the true interpreter and ruler of the future. He sends the dreams, gives the meaning, and brings both to pass. He also governs the delay, ordaining that Joseph wait longer, teaching that God's people are sustained by His remembrance rather than by the gratitude of others.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel echoes that God reveals mysteries and interprets dreams. Luke records two criminals crucified with Jesus, one crying remember me. Psalm 105 shows God's word testing Joseph until the appointed time of his release.
basic.oneStory: This chapter moves Joseph one step closer to the throne, even as it ends in apparent disappointment. God is arranging the pieces, revealing His power over the future and preparing the moment when He, not a forgetful cupbearer, will lift Joseph up to save many lives.

context.literary:
Genesis 40 is built as a pair of matched panels. The cupbearer tells his dream, verses 9 to 11, and Joseph interprets it, verses 12 to 13; the baker tells his dream, verses 16 to 17, and Joseph interprets it, verses 18 to 19. The two interpretations open with the same formula, 'This is the interpretation,' and the same arithmetic, three branches and three baskets are three days. The listener is lulled by the likeness until the last words of verse 19 turn the pattern inside out. The narrator has set the scene so that the difference lands with full weight.

Between the two panels stands Joseph's personal appeal, verses 14 and 15. It is the only place in the chapter where the story slows down to let Joseph speak about himself, and it is the first time in the whole narrative that he tells anyone what has been done to him. The plea is then answered by the closing verse in a double statement, 'did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him,' verse 23. The chapter ends not on the fulfilled dreams but on a man left behind.

The chapter also carries forward the pattern of Genesis 39. There Joseph was placed over Potiphar's house and then over the prison, Genesis 39:4 and 39:22, and here he is again a servant to his superiors, 'their personal attendant,' verse 4, using the same verb as in Potiphar's house. Dreams come in pairs throughout the Joseph story: Joseph's own two dreams in Genesis 37:5-9, the two officials' dreams here, and Pharaoh's two dreams in Genesis 41. Each pair raises the stakes, from a family, to two royal servants, to a nation and the world.

Finally, the chapter is a hinge of timing. It opens with 'Some time later,' verse 1, and it prepares for 'After two full years had passed,' Genesis 41:1. The reader learns to measure Joseph's story in God's time, not in the hopes of a prisoner.
context.historical:
The two prisoners are senior figures at court. The Hebrew calls them the 'chief' of the cupbearers and the 'chief' of the bakers, men who oversaw the king's drink and food. Such posts were offices of close personal trust, because the one who handled the king's cup and bread could reach the king himself. Nehemiah, centuries later, would hold the same office of cupbearer to a Persian king, Nehemiah 1:11. The chapter never says what the two men did, only that they 'offended their master,' verse 1, and that Pharaoh 'was angry,' verse 2. Their being held together while the matter was examined suggests an inquiry into a single incident.

They are confined in 'the house of the captain of the guard,' verse 3, the title that Genesis 39:1 gives to Potiphar. Joseph's prison is therefore still within the orbit of the household where he was first sold, and his work there is again the work of a servant.

Egypt took dreams seriously. Egyptian dream manuals survive that list dream images with their good or bad meanings, and interpreting dreams was a learned art practiced by trained specialists. That is the background to the officials' distress in verse 8: 'there is no one to interpret them.' Shut in prison, they had no access to the experts. Joseph's answer does not offer himself as a better expert; he points past all expertise to God.

The baker's sentence would have sounded especially terrible in Egypt. Egyptians went to great lengths to preserve the body for the life to come, and the prospect of a corpse left exposed for birds to eat was a horror beyond death itself. Royal occasions such as a birthday feast were natural moments for a king to settle outstanding cases in public, and verse 20 describes exactly that: a feast before 'all his officials,' with mercy for one and judgment for the other.
context.canonical:
The confession of verse 8, that interpretations belong to God, is taken up almost word for word in the career of Daniel, another Hebrew exile at a foreign court. Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar that no wise man or magician can explain the mystery, 'But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries,' Daniel 2:27-28, and the king himself ends by calling Daniel's God 'the Revealer of Mysteries,' Daniel 2:47. The Aramaic word Daniel uses for interpretation is a close cousin of the Hebrew word in Genesis 40.

Psalm 105 retells this season of Joseph's life as a time of testing. They bruised his feet with shackles and placed his neck in irons, 'until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right,' Psalm 105:18-19. The psalmist sees the prison not as an interruption of God's plan but as the furnace in which God's word refined His servant.

The forgotten benefactor becomes a wisdom theme. Ecclesiastes 9:15 tells of a poor wise man who saved his city, 'Yet no one remembered that poor man.' The phrase 'lift up the head' reappears at the very end of Kings, where a Babylonian king releases Jehoiachin from prison, gives him new clothes and a seat at the royal table, 2 Kings 25:27-29. Kings closes on a Joseph-like note of hope for the house of David.

The New Testament does not quote Genesis 40, but its shape reappears at Calvary, where two criminals die beside Jesus and one pleads, 'Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!' Luke 23:42. And Hebrews turns the forgotten prisoner into a standing duty for the church: 'Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them,' Hebrews 13:3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to learn that the future is not locked away in the libraries of Egypt's experts. The God of a Hebrew slave holds it, and He can make it known to His servant in a dungeon as easily as in a palace. For a people who would one day live as slaves in that same land, the lesson mattered. Egypt's power was real, but it did not own the meaning of history.

He also wanted them to see the character of God's servant under pressure. Joseph is attentive to the distress of others, verse 7, honest about God, verse 8, truthful even when the truth is fatal, verse 19, and candid about his own wrongs suffered, verse 15. He tells the baker the worst without softening it, which is itself a mark of a true prophet.

Most of all, the author wants the reader to feel the waiting. The chapter ends with a man forgotten, and the next chapter opens two full years later. Israel would know long seasons when God's promises seemed stalled, in Egypt, in the wilderness and in exile. Genesis 40 teaches them that God's delays are not His forgetfulness, and that when rescue comes it will be plainly His.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records a particular gift given to Joseph at a particular point in redemptive history. It does not teach believers to seek meaning in their dreams or to set up as interpreters. The line that carries across is Joseph's confession, that meaning and the future belong to God, and that confession warns against every attempt to read the future by technique.

What is modelled rather than commanded is worth noticing too. Joseph speaks up for justice in his own case, verse 15, without bitterness or slander; he names what was done to him without naming his brothers or Potiphar's wife. He uses ordinary means, asking the cupbearer for help, and the text does not rebuke him for it. Believers may likewise pursue lawful remedies against injustice, while resting their hope in God's timing. The cupbearer's failure is also instructive: gratitude that forgets its benefactor is a quiet sin, and Hebrews 13:3 turns remembering prisoners into a Christian duty.

debates.question: Was Joseph's request that the cupbearer remember him a lapse of faith or a proper use of means?

views.label: A proper, humble use of means
views.case: Asking for help is not unbelief. Joseph honestly states his innocence, verse 15, and seeks a lawful path out of unjust imprisonment, trusting God while acting wisely. The narrator attaches no rebuke to the request; the fault the text underlines in verse 23 is the cupbearer's forgetting, not Joseph's asking. Paul likewise appealed to his rights as a citizen, Acts 25:11, without any hint of distrust.

views.label: A momentary leaning on man
views.case: Some older interpreters saw Joseph's plea, followed by two more years in prison, as a gentle lesson that his rescue would come from God's hand and timing rather than a courtier's favour. On this reading the delay of Genesis 41:1 teaches Joseph, and the reader, to look past human patrons.

debates.bearing: Both agree that God's providence, not the cupbearer, secures Joseph's freedom. Since the text itself does not criticise Joseph, it is wiser not to add a fault. Believers may use ordinary means while resting their final hope in God, who remembers His own at the right time.

debates.question: What exactly is the baker's sentence in verse 19?

views.label: Beheading, then public display
views.case: Pharaoh will 'lift off your head,' literally lift your head from upon you, and then 'hang you on a tree,' with birds eating the flesh. Read in sequence, the baker is executed by beheading and his body is then displayed, a practice also seen in Joshua 10:26 and 1 Samuel 31:10, and anticipated in Deuteronomy 21:22, where the body of an executed man is hung up.

views.label: Impalement as the means of death
views.case: The BSB footnote offers 'impale you on a pole,' and impalement is attested as a form of execution in the ancient Near East. On this view 'lift off your head' is a grim wordplay on verse 13 rather than a separate act, and the hanging itself is the execution.

debates.bearing: The details differ, but the meaning does not. The baker dies in disgrace, his body exposed as a sign of the king's judgment. That picture of a man hung on wood under a sentence is the background to Deuteronomy 21:23 and to Paul's statement that Christ became a curse for us, Galatians 3:13.

study.originalLanguages:
The root behind 'interpret' and 'interpretation,' the verb patar and the noun pithron, is found in the Hebrew Bible only in the Joseph chapters, Genesis 40 and 41. It becomes a key word of this movement, sounding again and again through chapter 40. Its Aramaic relative, pesher, is the word Daniel uses when he gives Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar the meaning of what they saw, Daniel 2 and 5. The two books share not only a theme but a vocabulary: meaning is something God gives, not something the expert extracts.

The chapter's central pun rests on the idiom nasa rosh, to lift up the head. In verse 13 it means to restore to honour, as in Psalm 3:3, where God is 'the One who lifts my head,' and in 2 Kings 25:27, where the Hebrew says that the king of Babylon lifted up the head of Jehoiachin, which the BSB renders 'released.' In verse 19 Joseph uses the very same words and adds 'from upon you,' so that lifting the head becomes removing it. Verse 20 then uses the phrase once more, neutrally, of both men: Pharaoh 'lifted up the heads' of the cupbearer and the baker, that is, he called their cases. One expression holds honour, judgment and summons all at once.

The language of memory runs underneath the whole chapter. In verse 14 Joseph asks the cupbearer to 'remember me,' from zakar, and then to 'mention' him to Pharaoh, which is the causative form of the same verb, literally 'cause me to be remembered.' Verse 23 answers with a doubled verdict, 'did not remember... he forgot,' using shakach, the ordinary verb for forgetting. When the cupbearer finally speaks in Genesis 41:9, 'Today I recall my failures,' he uses the causative of zakar again. Against this human forgetting stands the Genesis pattern of divine remembering: 'God remembered Noah,' Genesis 8:1, and, closest to Joseph, 'God remembered Rachel,' his own mother, Genesis 30:22.

Joseph asks the cupbearer to 'show me kindness,' and the word is chesed, loyal love. It is exactly the word used for what the LORD had shown Joseph in the prison, 'the LORD was with him and extended kindness to him,' Genesis 39:21. Joseph asks a man for the kindness God has already given; the man withholds it, and God does not.

In verse 15 Joseph says 'I was kidnapped,' and the Hebrew doubles the verb, 'stolen, I was stolen,' the same intensive pattern the narrator used for 'you will surely die' in Genesis 2:17. Kidnapping was a capital crime under Israel's law, Exodus 21:16. Joseph also calls the prison a 'dungeon,' bor, the word for the pit his brothers threw him into, Genesis 37:24. His life has moved from one bor to another, and Genesis 41:14 will use the same word when he is brought out.

Finally, the officials' offence in verse 1 is expressed with chata, the common verb for sin, used here of a servant failing his master. And their 'downcast' faces in verse 7 are literally 'bad' faces, the same expression the Persian king uses of Nehemiah's sad face, Nehemiah 2:2.

typology.type: Two condemned men, one restored and one executed
typology.fulfillment: At Pharaoh's feast two men under the king's displeasure go out to opposite ends on the same day. At Calvary 'two robbers were crucified with Him, one on His right hand and the other on His left,' Matthew 27:38, and they too go to opposite ends. The escalation is decisive. In Egypt the outcome rested on a king's whim, and Joseph could only announce it; at the cross the dividing line is the criminals' response to Jesus Himself, Luke 23:39-43, and Jesus does not merely foretell the outcome but grants it. The type falls short because the cupbearer's restoration was a return to earthly service, while the penitent thief is promised Paradise.

Joseph asks the man who is about to be restored, 'please remember me,' verse 14, and the man forgets, verse 23. At the cross the roles are reversed: a guilty man asks the innocent One, 'Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!' Luke 23:42, and he is answered at once, 'today you will be with Me in Paradise.' Joseph's plea exposes the limits of human memory; the thief's plea meets a King whose memory is covenant faithfulness, like the God who remembered Noah and Rachel, Genesis 8:1 and 30:22. The type falls short in that Joseph asked for his own release, whereas Jesus, while granting release to another, stayed on the cross.

Joseph insists that 'even here I have done nothing' to deserve the dungeon, verse 15, yet he is counted among the king's offenders. Isaiah foretold a Servant who 'was numbered with the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:12, and Jesus applied that very line to Himself on the night of His arrest, Luke 22:37. The thief's words, 'this man has done nothing wrong,' Luke 23:41, are the verdict Joseph could only claim for himself. The escalation is that Joseph's innocence was relative, a young man wronged, while Christ's is absolute, and His place among transgressors was chosen, so that He 'bore the sin of many.'

typology.type: The third day and the lifting up
typology.fulfillment: The chapter turns on three days and a lifting up. Scripture elsewhere uses the third day as a day of God's decisive action, 'on the third day He will raise us up,' Hosea 6:2, and Paul says Christ 'was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:4. Jesus spoke of being 'lifted up from the earth,' John 12:32, a lifting that was both His cross and His exaltation. The New Testament never cites Genesis 40, so this is an echo rather than a declared type. It also falls short: in Egypt one man was lifted to honour and another to death, but in Christ one Man was lifted to death so that others might be lifted to life.

typology.type: The man hung on a tree
typology.fulfillment: The baker is hung on a tree and left exposed, the public sign of a king's judgment, verse 19. Israel's law later declared that 'anyone who is hung on a tree is under God's curse,' Deuteronomy 21:23, and Paul uses that verse to explain the cross: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. This is a correspondence of contrast. The baker hung for his own offence; Christ hung for the offences of others. The baker's body was left for the birds; Christ's body was buried the same day and raised on the third.

study.christ:
Genesis 40 leads to Christ first by pattern. Joseph is the innocent sufferer placed among the guilty, the servant who serves even in chains, and the one through whom a word of life and a word of death go out on the same day. Luke's account of the crucifixion gives the same scene a final and far greater form. Two criminals hang beside Jesus, one mocking, one pleading, and the division between them is drawn not by Pharaoh's mood but by how each responds to the One in the middle, Luke 23:39-43.

The pattern turns on the word remember. Joseph asked to be remembered by a man who forgot him. The penitent thief asked to be remembered by Jesus, and Jesus answered with a promise the cupbearer could never have given: 'today you will be with Me in Paradise,' Luke 23:43. Human memory fails the prisoner in Genesis; the memory of the crucified King does not. In Scripture God's remembering is His faithfulness in action, as when 'God remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,' Exodus 2:24, and in Christ that faithfulness reaches a dying criminal.

It leads to Christ by contrast in the matter of the curse. The baker is hung on a tree as a sign of royal judgment, and the Law would later say that such a man is under God's curse, Deuteronomy 21:23. Paul says Christ took that place deliberately: He 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. Where the baker bore his own guilt, Christ bore ours. Isaiah had foreseen a Servant 'numbered with the transgressors' who 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12, and Jesus claimed that text for Himself, Luke 22:37.

It leads to Christ by promise in the matter of timing. Joseph's rescue was delayed until God's appointed hour, and Psalm 105:19 says the word of the LORD tested him until it came true. Jesus too spoke of an hour appointed by the Father, and Paul says God sent His Son 'when the time had fully come,' Galatians 4:4. The waiting servant anticipates the Son who submitted Himself to the Father's timetable.

The motifs of three days and lifting up are best held lightly. The New Testament never quotes this chapter, so the reader should not press every detail, the vine, the cup, the baskets, into a hidden picture of the passion. What can be said with confidence is that God's pattern of bringing life out of apparent defeat on the third day, Hosea 6:2, comes to its fullness when Christ is 'raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:4.

And Joseph's plea gives the church its own duty. Christ counts service to the imprisoned as service to Himself, and Hebrews calls believers to 'remember those in prison as if you were bound with them,' Hebrews 13:3. Those remembered by Christ must not become forgetful cupbearers.
study.god:
The chapter reveals God first as the Lord of meaning. The officials assume that dreams need experts; Joseph assumes they need God. His question in verse 8 is not a boast about his own skill but a statement about ownership: the sense of events, like the events themselves, belongs to God. That is why Joseph can say the hardest word to the baker without hedging. He is not guessing. Isaiah 46:10 gives the doctrine its later form: God declares 'the end from the beginning.'

God is also sovereign over the smallest details. He gives two men two dreams on the same night, verse 5, each fitted to its dreamer, with numbers that match the exact date of Pharaoh's birthday. He brings the officials into the very prison where Joseph serves and assigns them to him, verse 4. None of this is announced as miracle, yet the narrator leaves the reader in no doubt that nothing here is accidental. Proverbs 16:9 says it plainly: 'A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps.'

The God of this chapter is present without being named in the action. The LORD 'was with' Joseph in the prison, Genesis 39:21 and 39:23, and chapter 40 shows what that presence looks like: not immediate release, but faithfulness, insight and usefulness inside confinement. God's presence does not always remove His people from hardship; it sustains them in it.

He holds together His goodness and His delay. The chapter ends with Joseph forgotten, and God permits two further years to pass, Genesis 41:1. That is a real tension, and Scripture does not hide it; the psalmists cry, 'How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?' Psalm 13:1. Yet the delay has purpose. Had the cupbearer spoken at once, Joseph might have been released as an obscure slave; instead he is remembered at the exact moment Pharaoh needs an interpreter. God's timing turns a prisoner's release into a nation's rescue.

He is the God who remembers. Genesis speaks of God remembering at every turning point, Noah in the flood, Genesis 8:1, and Rachel in her barrenness, Genesis 30:22, and He does not forget Joseph, whatever the cupbearer does. Isaiah would later put it tenderly: 'Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!' Isaiah 49:15.

He is also just. The baker's end is not presented as cruelty on God's part but as the outcome of a king's judgment that God foreknew and disclosed. The same God who restores also judges, and He tells the truth about both.

For worship, the chapter invites trust that does not depend on visible progress. It teaches believers to bring their confusion to God rather than to the experts of their age, to tell the truth even when it is hard, and to wait for the Lord who keeps His own scroll of remembrance, Malachi 3:16.

crossReferences.note: The frame for chapter 40. The LORD was with Joseph in the prison and 'extended kindness to him,' using chesed, the very word Joseph asks the cupbearer to show him in 40:14. God has already given the loyal love that the forgetful official will withhold.

Joseph calls his prison a 'dungeon,' bor, in 40:15, the same word as the empty pit into which his brothers threw him. His story runs from pit to pit until Genesis 41:14, when he is brought up out of the bor and into Pharaoh's presence.

The cupbearer finally speaks, 'Today I recall my failures,' using the causative form of the verb Joseph used when he asked to be mentioned. His retelling confirms that everything happened just as Joseph said, and it opens the way to Pharaoh's court.

The psalmist retells Joseph's imprisonment, feet bruised by shackles and neck in irons, 'until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right.' The waiting of Genesis 40 is read as God's word testing and vindicating His servant.

Daniel, another Hebrew at a foreign court, tells the king that no wise man or magician can explain the mystery, 'But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.' It is Joseph's question in 40:8 turned into a confession before a pagan king.

Two criminals hang beside Jesus and meet opposite ends. One pleads, 'Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!' and receives the promise of Paradise that very day. Where the cupbearer forgot Joseph, the crucified King remembers the one who asks.

The law of the executed man whose body is hung on a tree, who must be buried the same day because he is under God's curse. It gives covenant meaning to the baker's fate in 40:19 and prepares for Paul's use of it in Galatians 3:13.

Paul quotes Deuteronomy, 'Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree,' to explain that Christ redeemed us by becoming a curse for us. The baker was hung for his own offence; Christ was hung for the offences of others.

Kings ends with a Babylonian king releasing Jehoiachin from prison, changing his prison clothes and giving him a place at the royal table. The Hebrew says the king lifted up Jehoiachin's head, the idiom of Genesis 40:13, sounding a Joseph-like note of hope for David's line.

A poor wise man saves his city by his wisdom, 'Yet no one remembered that poor man.' The Teacher names the same bitter experience as Genesis 40:23: those who serve others well are often forgotten by those they helped.

'Then God remembered Rachel,' and she conceived Joseph. The verb zakar ties Joseph's birth to God's remembering, and it stands in quiet contrast with the cupbearer who 'did not remember Joseph.' The God who remembered the mother will remember the son.

'Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them.' The cupbearer's failure becomes the church's warning. Believers who have been remembered by Christ are called to carry imprisoned and mistreated brothers and sisters in their memory, prayer and practical care.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 40 sits deep in the long middle of the patriarchal story, where the promises to Abraham seem most at risk. God had promised land, seed and blessing to the nations, Genesis 12:3, and He had shown Joseph in two dreams that his family would bow before him, Genesis 37:5-9. Now the dreamer is a slave in a foreign prison, forgotten by the one man who could help him. The chapter answers the question every reader of Genesis has to face: can God's word survive human treachery, injustice and forgetfulness? It can, and here it does so in the dark.

The chapter looks back to the fall as well. Since Genesis 3 human life has been marked by broken trust, and here it shows in small ways: servants who offend their master, a king's anger, a man stolen from his homeland, a benefactor forgotten. Joseph's world is the world outside Eden. Yet the God who came looking in the garden is still at work, and He is working through a prisoner.

The chapter sets up what follows. The cupbearer's forgotten promise becomes the very channel of Joseph's rise, Genesis 41:9-14, and the gift of interpretation shown here to two men will be shown to Pharaoh and, through him, used to save 'many people,' Genesis 50:20. The descent of Joseph into Egypt is the first step in the descent of all Israel, which God had already announced to Abraham: 'your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not their own,' Genesis 15:13. The prison is part of the road to the Exodus.

Across the whole Bible the pattern of this chapter grows: the righteous sufferer, counted with the guilty, vindicated in God's time. Psalm 105 sings it of Joseph. Isaiah sees it in the Servant who was 'numbered with the transgressors.' It reaches its fullness in Christ, who hung between two criminals, promised Paradise to one of them, and was raised on the third day.

The new creation is the end of forgetting. Those who fear the LORD are written in a scroll of remembrance, Malachi 3:16, and the thief who asked to be remembered is with Christ in Paradise. The story that includes a forgotten prisoner ends with a multitude from every nation standing before the throne, Revelation 7:9, none of them forgotten, all of them fed, and every prison door opened.

quiz.q: How does Joseph respond when the prisoners say no one can interpret their dreams?

options.text: He asks, do not interpretations belong to God, then offers to hear them.
options.note: He points away from himself to God as the true interpreter, verse 8.

options.text: He boasts of his own skill in reading dreams.
options.note: He credits God, not himself; the point is God's revelation.

options.text: He refuses to get involved with their dreams.
options.note: He willingly hears and interprets, trusting God to give the meaning.

options.text: He tells them dreams are meaningless.
options.note: He treats the dreams as God's genuine disclosure of the future.

quiz.q: What happened to the two officials, just as Joseph foretold?

options.text: The cupbearer was restored and the baker executed, within three days.
options.note: Both came to pass on Pharaoh's birthday, verses 20 to 22.

options.text: Both were restored to their positions.
options.note: Only the cupbearer was restored; the baker was executed.

options.text: Both were executed for offending Pharaoh.
options.note: Only the baker died; the cupbearer was reinstated.

options.text: Both were released and forgotten.
options.note: One was restored and one killed, exactly as interpreted.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the cupbearer forgetting Joseph?

options.text: It shows human memory fails, but God will remember Joseph in His own time.
options.note: The delay ensures Joseph's rise is clearly God's doing, not a courtier's favor.

options.text: It proves Joseph's interpretation was wrong.
options.note: The interpretation came true; the forgetting is a separate, human failing.

options.text: It means God had abandoned Joseph.
options.note: God had not abandoned him; He was arranging a greater deliverance.

options.text: It ends Joseph's story permanently.
options.note: The story continues; the cupbearer remembers him in the next chapter.

quiz.q: How does this prison scene foreshadow the cross of Christ?

options.text: Two condemned men meet opposite ends, and one pleads to be remembered.
options.note: It echoes the two criminals beside Jesus and the thief's cry, Luke 23.

options.text: Joseph offers a sacrifice to atone for the prisoners.
options.note: There is no sacrifice here; the parallel is the two destinies and the plea to be remembered.

options.text: Pharaoh releases all prisoners in an act of mercy.
options.note: Pharaoh restores one and executes another; there is no general release.

options.text: The chapter has no connection to the cross.
options.note: Its echoes of two condemned men, remember me, and the third day point to Calvary.

quiz.q: What does the chapter teach about God and the future?

options.text: God alone reveals and controls the future, including its timing.
options.note: He sends the dreams, gives their meaning, and fulfills them on the third day.

options.text: The future is shaped mainly by skilled human interpreters.
options.note: Joseph insists interpretation belongs to God, not to human skill.

options.text: The future is random and cannot be known.
options.note: God knows and discloses it precisely in this chapter.

options.text: Egyptian diviners hold the true knowledge of dreams.
options.note: The chapter sets Israel's God above Egypt's diviners.

questions: Joseph gave God the credit before he said a word about the dreams. Where do you need to point away from your own ability and toward God in the gifts others praise in you?
Joseph served two hurting men faithfully even while imprisoned himself. How can your own hard place become a place of noticing and helping others?
The cupbearer forgot Joseph, and God's timing stretched on. How do you keep trusting God when your hopes are pinned on people who let you down?
One prisoner was restored and one condemned on the same day. How does this sober picture of two destinies shape the way you think about your standing before God?
The dying thief's plea, remember me, was answered by Christ. What does it mean to you that Jesus remembers and receives those the world forgets?

translationNotes.note: Lift up your head is a Hebrew idiom for showing favor and restoring to honor; the same phrase is turned to a grim sense in verse 19, lift off your head, heightening the contrast between the two fates.
Hang you on a tree may also be rendered impale you on a pole; the point is public execution followed by the shame of exposure to the birds.
In their presence he lifted up the heads of both officials draws together the two meanings of the idiom, one lifted to honor and one to execution, on the same day.
